planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; calafate tolerates poor rocky ground and coastal wind once established and needs little supplemental feeding.

directions: Calafate is a spiny, semi-evergreen Patagonian shrub bearing small, golden-yellow spring flowers followed by dusky blue-black berries with a tart, slightly sweet, faintly spicy flavor traditionally gathered by Mapuche and Patagonian settler communities for jams, syrups, and a regional liqueur. Folklore holds that anyone who eats a calafate berry is destined to return to Patagonia. Plant in full sun to light part shade on a well-drained slope or bank; established shrubs tolerate wind, drought, and poor stony soil far better than richer garden ground. Prune lightly after fruiting only to remove dead wood, since flowers and fruit form on older growth and heavy pruning reduces the next season's crop.
sources: Chilean Ministry of Agriculture — Native Fruit Species of Patagonia
Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Berberis of South America

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in well-drained, average garden soil; Korean barberry is unfussy about soil pH and establishes readily in full sun to light shade.

directions: Korean barberry is a dense, extremely cold-hardy deciduous shrub from the Korean peninsula, grown for drooping clusters of fragrant yellow spring flowers, brilliant scarlet-red fall foliage, and bright red, elongated fruit that persists into winter. The tart berries are edible cooked into jelly or syrup in the same manner as European barberry, though they are astringent eaten raw. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for cereal stem rust, check local agricultural extension guidance before planting near wheat, barley, or oat fields. Give the shrub full sun for the best fall color and fruit set, though it tolerates part shade; little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood in late winter.
sources: USDA Forest Service — Fire Effects Information System, Berberis koreana
Morton Arboretum — Plant Clinic Shrub Guide

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, chalky to neutral soil; European serviceberry is naturally found on limestone slopes and tolerates lean, alkaline ground better than most fruiting shrubs.

directions: European serviceberry is a compact, multi-stemmed shrub native to the mountains and limestone hills of central and southern Europe, producing clouds of star-shaped white flowers in April followed by small, sweet, blue-black berries in midsummer that ripen a few weeks after the flowers fade. The fruit is traditionally eaten fresh, dried like currants, or made into preserves in Alpine and Mediterranean regions, with a mild flavor similar to a mellow blueberry. It thrives on thin, stony, alkaline soils where richer-feeding shrubs struggle, and tolerates part shade along a woodland edge as well as full sun. Established plants need only occasional thinning of old wood to keep the shrub open and productive.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Amelanchier Species Guide
Plants for a Future Database — Amelanchier ovalis

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade; include at least one male plant for every 5-6 female plants to ensure fruit set.

directions: Chilean pernettya is a low, spreading, needle-leaved evergreen shrub from the temperate rainforest understory of Chile and Argentina, producing marble-sized berries in shades of white, pink, magenta, or deep purple that persist on the plant from autumn well into winter. The mild, faintly sweet berries are edible fresh, though they are grown mainly as a striking woodland-garden ornamental with genuinely edible fruit rather than a production crop. Like other ericaceous shrubs it requires acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and is happiest in the dappled shade of taller shrubs or trees, where it colonizes slowly by suckering to form a dense groundcover. The species is dioecious, so a male pollinator plant must be grown nearby for the showier female selections to fruit heavily.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Gaultheria mucronata Cultivation Notes
Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Flora of Chile Gaultheria Account

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade, mimicking the cool forest-floor conditions of its native range.

directions: Kamchatka bilberry is a mat-forming, creeping deciduous subshrub from the cool forests of northeastern Asia, Japan, and Kamchatka, spreading by underground rhizomes to just a few inches tall. Its bright red, translucent berries are famous among foragers in its native range for an intense, pineapple-like fragrance and flavor unlike any other Vaccinium, traditionally eaten fresh or preserved in Japanese and Russian Far East folk cuisine. Extremely cold-hardy and adapted to short, cool growing seasons, it performs best as a shaded woodland-floor groundcover in consistently moist, peaty, acidic soil and struggles in hot summer climates. Once established it needs little care beyond an annual topdressing of leaf mold or pine needle mulch to maintain soil acidity.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Vaccinium Germplasm Collection Notes
Flora of Japan — Ericaceae, Vaccinium praestans

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to part shade, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun.

directions: Tasmanian waxberry is an upright evergreen understory shrub from the cool temperate rainforests of Tasmania, bearing small white spring flowers followed by plump, waxy-white to pale pink berries that were eaten fresh by Tasmanian Aboriginal peoples and remain a foraged bush food today. The berries have a mild, watery-sweet flavor and are best enjoyed fresh rather than processed. As a true rainforest-floor species it needs the cool, humid, sheltered conditions of a shaded woodland garden with consistently moist, acidic soil and protection from drought and strong sun, making it a good companion for rhododendrons and other broadleaf evergreens. Mulch annually with leaf litter or pine bark to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and avoid any hint of summer drought, which quickly stresses the shallow root system.
sources: Tasmanian Herbarium — Gaultheria hispida Species Profile
Australian National Botanic Gardens — Australian Native Bush Food Plants
